author: clara-bennett
title: When You Reach for the Phone to Call Her
dek: Grief does not wait for anniversaries. Sometimes it arrives in a parking lot, with your hand already reaching for her number.
pull_quote: Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit.
body_html:
It happens on a Tuesday, or a Sunday afternoon, or in a grocery store parking lot. Something small goes right, or something small goes wrong, and your hand is already moving toward the phone.

You know exactly what you were going to say. You can almost hear how she would answer. The way she said your name when she picked up. The little pause before she asked how you were really doing.

And then you remember.

The phone is still in your hand. Her number is probably still in it, too. You may not have been able to delete it. Nobody needs to know that.

The ordinary moments are the hardest

People expect grief to show up at the funeral, on her birthday, on Mother's Day. It does. But it also arrives in places no one warned you about.

The recipe you cannot quite remember. The song in a waiting room. The sweater on a stranger that looks like one she wore. The good news you want to tell someone, and the only someone you want is her.

These moments are quiet. Nobody around you notices them. You stand in the cereal aisle with your heart dropping through the floor, and the world keeps going.

Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit.

Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit. For years, maybe decades, she was the person you called. Your hand remembers that, even when the rest of you knows better.

You do not have to stop reaching. You do not have to train yourself out of it. There is nothing here to fix.

Letting the moment be what it is

Some days, the remembering knocks the breath out of you. Some days, it is softer, almost tender, like she was close for a second. Both are real. Neither one means you are doing this wrong.

If you want, you can let the moment have a place to go. A page. A notebook in your bag. A note on your phone that starts with her name. You can write down the thing you were going to tell her, exactly the way you would have said it.

She does not get to answer. That is the part that hurts. But the words still belong to her, and you can still give them somewhere to land.

You are not behind. You are not stuck. You are someone who loved her mother and still does, in the middle of an ordinary day.

A gentle prompt: Think of the last time you reached for the phone to call her. What were you going to tell her? Write it to her now, the way you would have said it out loud.

Clara's journals for daughters who lost their mother are on the way, with more pages for moments like this one.

author: clara-bennett
title: Keeping Her Close: Recipes, Handwriting, and Unsent Letters
dek: Her recipe cards, her handwriting, a letter that begins Dear Mom: small, quiet ways to keep your mother near.
pull_quote: A letter you never send is still a letter. She is still the one it is for.
body_html:
There is a drawer somewhere with her handwriting in it. A grocery list. A birthday card. A recipe card with a stain in the corner, from the year she made that dish for everyone.

You may not open the drawer often. Some days you cannot. Some days you open it just to see the way she wrote her capital letters.

That counts, too.

Her recipes, her hands, her kitchen

So much of a mother lives in the small, repeated things. The way she cut onions. The pan she always used. The note in the margin that says less salt or double this, in ink that has started to fade.

Cooking one of her recipes can feel like standing next to her. It can also feel unbearable. You might make it once and cry the whole time. You might not be ready to make it at all. There is no right time and no wrong one.

If you do cook it, you do not have to make it perfectly. Hers was never written down all the way anyway. Some of it was only in her hands.

A letter you never send is still a letter. She is still the one it is for.

Her handwriting is its own kind of keepsake. Some daughters frame a single line. Some tuck a card into the book they read at night. Some just keep it close, in a wallet or a jacket pocket, where it can be touched without being looked at.

Writing to her anyway

And then there are the things you never got to say. Or the things you said a hundred times and want to say once more.

A letter you never send is still a letter. She is still the one it is for. You can start with Dear Mom and write one sentence, or ten pages. You can tell her about your week. You can tell her you are angry. You can tell her you miss the way she hummed while she folded towels.

None of this is about moving on. It is about keeping a door open. Her recipes, her handwriting, your letters to her: these are small ways of saying she is still part of your life, because she is.

You do not need a ritual that looks a certain way. You only need something that feels like her.

A gentle prompt: Begin a letter with "Dear Mom," and tell her about one small thing that happened today. Something she would have wanted to hear about.

Clara's journals, including a recipe memory book and a book of letters to Mom, are on the way.
